items.title: As winter nears, heating oil emerges as hurdle for Republicans in US Senate races
items.author: Tim McLaughlin, Nichola Groom, Timothy Gardner, Leah Douglas
items.creator: Tim McLaughlin, Nichola Groom, Timothy Gardner, Leah Douglas
items.summary: It's a top issue in northern states with competitive Senate races as winter approaches.
items.body:
Eighty-year-old Rick Russman of New Hampshire spent five decades as a Republican. This year, as his state braces for a winter of soaring heating oil costs, he will vote for Democrat Chris Pappas in one of the country's most closely watched Senate races.
For Russman, a resident of Kingston, the situation has become so dire that he will rely on a wood stove to help heat his home this winter rather than on heating oil alone. "Fuel that costs more than $6 a gallon is a huge expense," he said.
High heating oil prices are a potent issue in northern states that depend on the fuel like Maine, New Hampshire and Alaska, which have competitive Senate races on November 3 that could determine whether Trump's fellow Republicans maintain control of Congress, according to Reuters interviews with 15 voters, candidates and strategists.
Democratic candidates have sought to tie the higher costs to Trump's war with Iran, which has disrupted global diesel supplies. The shortage drove prices for diesel, which is similar to heating oil, to a record high above $6.50 a gallon, making groceries and consumer staples more expensive.
Reuters was first to report this week that the US Energy Department [USN:L1N46700H TEXT:"released"] heating oil from reserves in the Northeast.
When asked about criticism that Trump's policies have led to soaring heating oil costs that could make Republicans vulnerable, the White House pointed to that fuel release, a move an analyst said was unlikely to affect prices.
Heating oil prices have climbed above $6 per gallon nationally, up from about $3.50 a year ago, according to the Energy Information Administration.
The costs are a headwind for Republicans, said Lance Dutson, a Republican strategist in Maine. "The party in power is held responsible for things like that, and it’s so clearly Trump’s fault because of this Iran war."
Nearly 80% of Americans [USN:L6N45T0W3 TEXT:"blame"] Trump policies for higher costs including energy, according to an October Reuters/Ipsos poll.
In New Hampshire, where 43% of residents use heating oil, Pappas said energy dominates voters' concerns as he challenges Republican John Sununu.
"Energy costs and heating oil prices are the beginning and end of every conversation I'm having on the campaign trail," Pappas said.
Sununu’s campaign did not respond to several requests for comment.
ALASKA EVEN HIGHER In Alaska, where roughly 30% of residents rely on heating oil, the issue has surfaced in the Senate race between Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola, who has campaigned on lowering energy costs.
In remote Alaska communities, fuel is often shipped long distances. Diesel also generates electricity and powers transportation, pushing up the cost of goods and services.
In the Yukon River community of St. Mary's, Mayor Sven Paukan said heating fuel has risen to about $10 per gallon, roughly $2 more than last year.
"It's pretty difficult to heat homes nowadays," Paukan said.
Sullivan said he supports a "temporary pause of American diesel exports," a policy [USN:SPN45A01C TEXT:"Trump has considered"]. A Peltola spokesperson said the Iran war had helped drive up heating fuel, gasoline and grocery costs in Alaska.
Sullivan has said he supports the war but that it should end soon, and this week he encouraged Alaska fishermen to apply for a new $8 billion Trump administration [USN:SPN4650BH TEXT:"program"] to offset diesel costs for farmers.
Suzanne Downing, former communications director for the Alaska Republican Party, said heating oil is a concern for Republicans. "Many people in Fairbanks ... pay more in the wintertime for their fuel bill than they do for their mortgage," she said. "The Iran war is being blamed for this."
MAINE 'DOUBLE WHAMMY' In Maine, where 54% of homes use heating oil, rising fuel costs have featured in the Senate race between Republican incumbent Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson.
The costs are even higher for fishermen and farmers who use diesel to power their motors and warm homes with oil. "For them, it really is a double whammy," said Mark Brewer, chair of the political science department at the University of Maine.
"Folks who probably have the lowest incomes are the ones who are facing the highest energy costs," said Scott Thistle, spokesperson for MaineHousing, the public housing authority, adding older housing stock and mobile homes are costlier to heat.
Gerry Cushman, a fifth-generation lobsterman from Port Clyde, said fishermen were already facing fluctuating prices for their catches.
But Cushman said he plans to support Collins, the Republican, arguing that her seniority and influence outweigh voters' frustrations.
"If you're a senior senator and you're head of (Senate Committee on Appropriations), you can get more done than a freshman senator,” he said.
Collins said after initially supporting the war she has voted several times to bring it to an end. She also pushed the US government to speed the release of $38 million for Maine from the $4 billion federal Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program and urged Trump to tap the heating oil reserve.
That's not enough for Maine lobsterman Dave Cousens of South Thomaston, who plans to vote for Jackson. Cousens blamed high energy costs on Trump's Iran war and said he will be forced to forgo a Florida vacation.
"He picked a fight with the wrong country, and we're all paying for it."

items.title: Divided over Israel, Detroit Democrats unite on rising costs for midterm elections
items.author: Heather Schlitz
items.creator: Heather Schlitz
items.summary: It was her son’s eighth birthday, but Dayna Broadnax could not afford a present.
items.body:
It was her son’s eighth birthday, but Dayna Broadnax could not afford a present.
Broadnax, a 42-year-old single mother of four in Detroit, said soaring gas and grocery prices left little money to pay the bills, let alone buy gifts or throw a birthday party.
“It’s hard to tell your kids that you don't have the funds right now to buy them a $3 bag of Skittles,” she said while watching her sons practice with a free basketball team at St. Suzanne Community Resource Center.
Ahead of the November 3 midterm elections, Broadnax’s concerns are widely shared in Detroit. Jewish, Muslim and Black voters interviewed by Reuters often put affordability ahead of disputes over Israel and Gaza, even as many expressed reservations about Democratic US Senate nominee [USN:L1N4420RK TEXT:"Abdul El-Sayed"].
El-Sayed, who could make history as the first Muslim US senator, faces former congressman Mike Rogers in a competitive race that could help determine control of the Senate. A RealClearPolitics average gives El-Sayed a two-point lead – 48% to 46%.
Broadnax has yet to decide who to support, saying she will vote for the candidate most focused on lowering costs.
She sometimes skips meals so her children can eat and chooses which bills to pay after gas eats up at least $50 of the $150 she makes on a typical day driving for Lyft.
“Being a single mom, trying to take care of four boys out here in America now is too hard,” she said. “Whatever candidate whose main focus is affordability – that’s who I’m going with.”
But El-Sayed faces resistance from some voters who would ordinarily be inclined to support a Democrat, particularly over Israel.
“Both of the candidates have decided that this election is about Abdul,” said Matt Grossmann, a political science professor at Michigan State University. “He needs to win over voters that would normally support the Democratic candidate and are upset with President Trump but might have reservations about him – personal or policy reservations.”
El-Sayed’s challenge is not only keeping uneasy Democrats from voting for Rogers, but getting them to vote at all. Some voters told Reuters that opposing Trump made backing Rogers difficult, while concerns about El-Sayed led others to consider sitting out the race.
JEWISH VOTERS’ RESERVATIONS Most Jewish voters in Detroit traditionally vote Democratic, but some have deep reservations about El-Sayed over his views on Israel, particularly his response to a March attack on a suburban synagogue. After a man rammed his truck into Temple Israel while more than 100 children were inside, El-Sayed drew backlash when he said “hurt people hurt people" in reference to the attacker.
Though El-Sayed later apologized for the comment, he has continued to draw heavy criticism from a community shaken by the attack.
Rabbi Aaron Starr of Congregation Shaarey Zedek said some Jewish men now cover their heads with baseball caps instead of yarmulkes because they fear being targeted if identified as Jews. Starr's synagogue spends twice as much on security measures for its sprawling campus following the attack.
Starr and a group of Jewish clergy launched a petition calling for the Democratic Party to agree to a set of “non-negotiable” principles, including acknowledging Israel’s right to exist and Jewish sovereignty in Israel. El-Sayed has not signed the petition or communicated with the group, Starr said. He said he would not vote for the Democratic nominee.
“He is hyper-focused on Israel and American supporters of the state of Israel and seemed to be placing an awful lot of blame on Israel for America's problems,” Starr said in his study, where “hurt people help people” yard signs leaned against a wall beside shelves of religious texts.
El-Sayed briefly campaigned with Hasan Piker, a left-wing streamer who has drawn criticism over comments about Israel and American Jews. The association has troubled some voters, while others remain more focused on the cost of living.
“I don't love the fact that he campaigned with Hasan Piker during the primary,” said Alicia Chandler, a 47-year-old Jewish Detroit resident and former supporter of El-Sayed's Democratic primary opponent Haley Stevens. “But it cost me almost $100 to fill my car with gas yesterday.”
El-Sayed has repeatedly pledged to protect Jewish people from antisemitism, saying in an August speech after winning the Democratic primary that his commitment to Jewish safety was “the same commitment that I have to the safety of my own daughters.”
GAZA AND THE POCKETBOOK In 2024, frustration with the Biden-Harris administration’s support for Israel’s war in Gaza drove many Arab American and Muslim voters in Michigan away from the Democratic ticket, with some backing the Republican Trump or third-party candidates and others choosing not to vote.
At Shibam Coffee, a Yemeni coffeehouse in the Arab-majority city of Dearborn, volunteers wearing “Abdul for Senate” shirts gathered over cardamom coffee, honeycomb bread and sambusas before heading out to canvass. The cafe is popular with young Arab Americans, many of whom now support El-Sayed.
Sumayah Dhalai, a 22-year-old senior at Wayne State University who plans to vote for El-Sayed, liked his policy position opposing funding for the Israeli government but said her fears about finding a job and affording rent and groceries were a bigger factor in deciding who to vote for.
“The overwhelming majority of us are very scared about graduating because everybody’s telling us that everything sucks,” Dhalai said. “As much as I want to say I'm out here fighting for world peace, I have to ensure my own ability to succeed before I can then turn to focus on everybody else's.”
While parts of Detroit have benefited from new investment, others have not, including the neighborhood housing St. Suzanne Community Resource Center, where the median household income is just $36,525 and roughly half the children live in poverty, according to US Census data.
“The financial stress is continual,” said Steve Wasko, the director of the center where Broadnax's sons play basketball. “Being able to pay your rent, afford your light bill, pay your mortgage, or pay to have your furnace working sufficiently – these are the most common requests that come through the door."

items.title: Five takeaways from Trump's midterm campaign rallies
items.author: Steve Holland, Bo Erickson, Nandita Bose, Jacob Bogage
items.creator: Steve Holland, Bo Erickson, Nandita Bose, Jacob Bogage
items.summary: Trump has long had a fixation on the human physique that stretches beyond the body politic.
items.body:
President Donald Trump is in the midst of a nationwide campaign blitz ahead of the November midterm elections, holding near-daily rallies to boost turnout for Republicans who are fighting to keep control of Congress.
In his 90-minute stump speeches, Trump defends his economic policies, boasts about crowd size, mocks protesters and has even admired a fellow Republican’s buttocks.
Here are five takeaways from Reuters coverage of the president’s appearances, staged mostly in Republican-friendly areas across the country:
TRUMP'S ECONOMIC PITCH COLLIDES WITH VOTER REALITY At the start of the month, Trump said he had done a “[USN:L1N45M10K TEXT:"bad job"]” explaining his economic record. He has tried to remedy that at his rallies, pointing to a record-low [USN:S0N4310A5 TEXT:"poverty rate"], low [USN:L1N45N170 TEXT:"unemployment,"] record highs in the [USN:L6N45S0IV TEXT:"stock market"] and cheaper prices for some food items.
But his sales pitch is colliding with voters' concerns about how much they are spending on gas, groceries and other everyday expenses.
Consumer prices accelerated in September as the cost of gasoline surged. The nationwide average price of gas is $4.27 per gallon ($1.13 per litre), nearly 40% higher than a year ago, according to AAA. Trump has repeatedly promised that gas prices will fall once the Iran war ends.
The disconnect was evident outside Trump's rally in rural Kansas, where Chester Daniel, a 90-year-old military veteran and Trump supporter, said the economy has “a long way to go” to help working people.
“Prices? Too high! We will never go back to what they were when this all started, but they need to come way down," Daniel said. "I don’t know how these young people make a living for their family."
RALLY MAP SHOWS REPUBLICANS PLAYING DEFENSE Trump's travel map signals just how difficult it will be for Republicans to retain control of Congress, with the president forced to play defense deep in conservative territory.
Trump has traveled twice to Texas for Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton, campaigned for Republican Senate incumbent Roger Marshall in Kansas and made two stops in Ohio for Senator Jon Husted. Trump also rallied for Republicans in competitive races in Alaska, Iowa, Montana and South Carolina. He is set to visit Mississippi on Monday.
Those are places Republicans are accustomed to winning easily, not battlegrounds where Trump would spend time during the crucial final weeks before an election.
Paxton narrowly trails Democrat James Talarico in polls, while Marshall faces a serious challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton in a state that has not elected a Democratic senator in nearly a century. Husted trails former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown in polls in Ohio, and Republican Senate hopeful Ashley Hinson is in a close race against Democrat Josh Turek in Iowa.
Notably absent from Trump's travels so far with less than two weeks until Election Day: Michigan, Maine, Minnesota and New Hampshire – also home to tight Senate races. He is soon poised to hit some of those locations. He is scheduled travel to Michigan on Sunday and has said he also plans to go to Maine.
TRUMP'S BOASTS ABOUT BIG CROWDS MEET UNEVEN REALITY Trump has made crowd sizes a recurring theme of his midterm rallies, portraying packed arenas and thousands of people he says are stranded outside as evidence of his persisting popularity.
But actual turnout on the campaign trail in recent weeks has been uneven. Some rallies have drawn capacity crowds but have shown little sign of the overflow Trump described. At others, large sections of seats remained empty even in modest-sized venues.
"I'm doing these every night, and no matter where I go, it's the same thing. It's massive crowds," Trump said at a rally in North Carolina on Tuesday. "We have big screens outside. Thousands and thousands of people. There's something going on that's very special."
The venue was filled to capacity, but there were no signs of crowds outside waiting to get in or watching on screens.
At an October 7 rally in San Antonio, Texas, Trump said lines stretched two miles outside the arena even as sizable sections inside remained empty.
Crowd sizes are not always an accurate measure of political support, but Trump has pointed to them as a sign of strength even as his approval rating has fallen to 31%, the lowest of either of his presidential terms, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll released on Monday.
Trump is not on the ballot on November 3. For Republican candidates, the question is whether the enthusiasm he generates among his supporters can translate into votes for them.
FRANCE BECOMES A 'BETE NOIRE' FOR MIDTERMS Trump has often used French President Emmanuel Macron as a foil in his campaign stump speeches, claiming he strong-armed Macron into raising prescription drug prices in France by threatening tariffs on a popular French export, champagne, and other goods.
But in the last week or so Trump has seized on another narrative about France, casting its violent unrest of recent weeks as a warning of what he says could happen in the US if Democrats win in the midterms. Trump has blamed the unrest on migrants and Muslims, following a familiar playbook that has featured in his politics for more than a decade.
“What the hell happened to France?” Trump told a crowd in a livestock competition arena in Clemson, South Carolina, on Wednesday.
Notably, the French protests have taken a larger role in Trump’s recent speeches than two other major foreign policy headaches he has been unable to resolve: Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and his war against Iran.
“They’ll end one way or another,” Trump said of the two conflicts at his Clemson rally. He did not elaborate on how they might end, but complained that he was not awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for his work to resolve conflicts around the world.
TRUMP PUTS THE BODY IN BODY POLITIC Trump has long had a fixation on the human physique that stretches beyond the body politic.
This campaign season, Trump has given particular attention to Husted, a 59-year-old former college football player for the University of Dayton.
At rallies in Ohio, Kentucky and North Carolina, Trump marveled at Husted’s physique, at one point saying his backside is “like a pile of muscle.”
“Then I looked at his legs, and I said, ‘Man, his feet are big.’ Then I looked at his shoulders, and I tapped him on the shoulder, and it actually hurt my hand. It was like a piece of steel. I said, ‘This guy’s a monster,’” Trump said.
Trump had similar praise on Friday for Robert F. Kennedy Jr., his secretary of health and human services, telling a campaign rally in Florida that the 72-year-old "has the body of a 30-year-old."
Such riffs are familiar terrain for Trump. At the close of his 2024 campaign, he used a Pennsylvania rally speech to tell a crude story about PGA legend Arnold Palmer's prowess beyond his golf game. Trump's focus over the years on people's physical attributes has also included mocking the weight and looks of his opponents.
Trump finds even some of his friends lacking in fashion sense, including the rumpled Paxton.
"Some may not like the way he dresses," Trump said about him at the Republicans' midterm convention in Dallas in mid-September, adding: "I don't."
That has not stopped Trump from campaigning for Paxton, however. He returns to Texas on Tuesday for two more campaign rallies.

items.title: L'Ukraine dit que Starlink refonctionne normalement
items.author: Reuters
items.creator: Reuters
items.summary: Le système de communication par satellites Starlink et sa version militaire Starshield fonctionnent à nouveau à des vitesses supérieures à 400 km/h, a déclaré samedi le ministre ukrainien de la Défense.
items.body:
Le système de communication par satellites Starlink et sa version militaire Starshield fonctionnent à nouveau à des vitesses supérieures à 400 km/h, a déclaré samedi le ministre ukrainien de la Défense.
Ces systèmes ont été perturbés pendant plus d'une semaine par des restrictions de service qui ont ralenti les connexions et affecté les opérations militaires de l'Ukraine contre la Russie.
"Les systèmes de surveillance du ministère de la Défense enregistrent un retour à une vitesse normale de Starlink/Starshield. Nous enregistrons une vitesse supérieure à 400 km/h. La connexion est stable", a dit Evhenii Khmara à des journalistes.
Le président Volodimir Zelensky a confirmé que Starlink et Starshield fonctionnaient de nouveau normalement depuis la nuit dernière. "C'est le plus important aujourd'hui", a-t-il sur l'application de messagerie Telegram.
Les restrictions à l'utilisation de Starlink, signalées pour la première fois le 14 octobre, ont affaibli les capacités ukrainiennes d'interception des drones russes et perturbé les communications sur la ligne de front, ont dit les responsables ukrainiens. Selon diverses sources, les vitesses de connexion avaient été réduites à 160 km/h voire moins.
Les problèmes de l'Ukraine avec le réseau Starlink, propriété de SpaceX, entreprise d'Elon Musk, sont apparus après l'annonce par le président américain Donald Trump d'un accord avec son homologue russe Vladimir Poutine sur la livraison par la Russie de diesel aux Etats-Unis et le blocage de nouvelles sanctions américaines contre Moscou. Donald Trump a simultanément exigé de l'Ukraine l'arrêt de ses bombardements contre les raffineries russes.
Ni Elon Musk ni l'exécutif américain n'ont admis être à l'origine de ces restrictions frappant l'Ukraine et tous deux ont publiquement déclaré qu'une telle décision ne pouvait être prise que par l'autre partie.
Reuters a rapporté que l'ordre de limiter l'exploitation de Starshield émanait de la Maison blanche.

items.title: Violence flares in Paris after largely peaceful protests across France
items.author: Juliette Jabkhiro, Yann Tessier, Crispian Balmer
items.creator: Juliette Jabkhiro, Yann Tessier, Crispian Balmer
items.summary: The interior minister mobilized 70,000 police nationwide, 10,000 more than on October 17, when vandalism and looting raised questions about the government's ability to maintain order.
items.body:
Hundreds of thousands of demonstrators marched in France on Saturday, with largely peaceful rallies giving way to clashes in Paris and Marseille as night fell despite a huge security operation aimed at preventing a repeat of [USN:L1N46608H TEXT:"last week's unrest"].
The Interior Ministry said 410,000 people took part in protests nationwide, though unions said the true figure was twice as high.
The main demonstration took place on the southeastern fringes of Paris, where at least 110,000 people turned out to denounce rising living costs and growing inequality.
The atmosphere deteriorated sharply after the rally ended. Riot police fired tear gas and water cannon at a group of around 500 hooded youths before they eventually dispersed on a cold, rainy evening.
In France's second city, Marseille, youths set fire to rubbish bins to block roads, and hurled rocks and bottles at security forces. Police said several stores, including two jewellery shops, were ransacked.
Clashes also flared in Lyon, Bordeaux, Grenoble, Clermont-Ferrand, Lille, Rennes, Nantes and Toulouse.
"In almost every march we saw the formation of these high-risk groups. They broke away from the main body and sought to commit acts of violence," said Interior Minister Laurent Nunez, accusing far-left activists and criminal gangs of seeking to foment trouble.
PARIS IN LOCKDOWN Authorities deployed 70,000 police officers and gendarmes, 10,000 more than a week earlier, after conceding they had underestimated the scale of the unrest on October 17.
Nunez told reporters the violence was less intense than a week ago, when looters and vandals went on the rampage. "What changed was anticipation," he said.
He also said far-right activists had sought confrontations with leftist groups in the southern cities of Nice and Montpellier, opening a potential new front in the disturbances.
Much of central Paris took on the appearance of a city under lockdown, with shopkeepers [USN:L2N46A00I TEXT:"boarding up storefronts"], [USN:L5N46A022 TEXT:"museums closing their doors"] and more than 20 metro stations shut.
Business groups urged retailers to remain closed after thousands of shops and businesses were damaged or looted across France last weekend.
"There are hardly any customers, so it's not really worth staying open," said Oskar, manager of a Kiton boutique in Paris.
Several of the capital's best-known cultural institutions, including the Louvre, the Musee d'Orsay and the Paris Opera, closed for the day as a precaution, leaving tourists frustrated.
"Everything's boarded up and we're not quite sure where we should be," said Xavier Dolliole, a tourist from the US city of New Orleans.
PROTESTS RIPPLE ACROSS EUROPE The nationwide disorder began with small student demonstrations in suburban Paris last month to denounce school conditions. It swiftly broadened into a wider protest against the government's economic policies and inspired demonstrations in neighbouring countries.
On Saturday [USN:L6N46A05C TEXT:"Belgian police"] used tear gas and pepper spray as they clashed in Brussels with anti-government demonstrators, with protests also taking place in a number of Italian cities for a second weekend, [USN:L2N46A02Y TEXT:"and in Albania"].
Hard-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon, who joined the Paris rally, predicted the protests would continue until President Emmanuel Macron, whose mandate expires next year, addressed the social malaise in France, one of the world's richest nations.
"Given the current situation, I think he will come to understand that this will happen again every week. There is still time for (Macron) to give in. After that, the only thing left to him will be the exit door," Melenchon told reporters.
FAR-RIGHT PARTY HOLDS CONGRESS Many demonstrators accused the government of overreacting to last week's turmoil, as soldiers were dispatched to patrol the Champs-Elysees, a grand boulevard lined with luxury shops and restaurants.
"We shed tears for shops, not for the people who are being impoverished all year round," said Clara Lebbadi, a 22-year-old arts student.
"My friend and I almost didn't come because we were scared, but we came precisely because it's important not to let repression win," she added.
The first authorised march on Saturday passed off peacefully in Orléans, around 120 km (75 miles) south of Paris, where demonstrators rallied against Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally, which is holding a party congress in the city.
A [USN:L6N4690NC TEXT:"shooting"] west of Paris on Friday heightened tensions. A gunman suspected of acting out of Islamophobic hatred killed one person and wounded four others, including a 12-year-old girl.
"We have come to tell the far right, face-to-face, that we are not afraid," said Bally Bagayoko, the mayor of Saint-Denis and a member of Melenchon's France Unbowed party.

Ukraine says Starlink and Starshield operating at 400 kph after week of throttling

KYIV, Oct 24 (Reuters) – The Starlink satellite communications system and its military version Starshield are operating again at speeds over 400 km per hour, Kyiv’s defence minister said on Saturday, after over a week of service restrictions that slowed connections and disrupted military operations.

“The Ministry of Defence’s monitoring systems are recording a return to normal speed for Starlink/Starshield. We are recording a speed of over 400 kph. The connection is stable,” Evhenii Khmara told reporters.

The Ukrainian military does not disclose the systems’ maximum operating speeds, and the defence ministry did not say whether service had been fully restored.

Show Full Article

“Monitoring systems had previously recorded disruptions to the Starlink/Starshield service. The speed metrics have now returned to normal,” the ministry said.

The restrictions, first reported on October 14, undermined Ukraine’s ability to intercept Russian attack drones and disrupted frontline communications, Ukrainian officials said. Sources said connection speeds had been reduced to about 160 kph or less.

Ukraine’s problems with SpaceX-owned Starlink came after US President Donald Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel and waived new sanctions on Moscow while pressing Ukraine to stop striking Russian oil refineries.

Neither SpaceX boss Elon Musk nor the US government has acknowledged responsibility for restricting Starlink or Starshield in Ukraine. Both have said publicly that any such decision could only have been taken by the other.

Reuters has reported that the order to throttle Starshield came from inside the White House.

Trump said on Friday that if problems with access to Starlink communications systems in Ukraine persisted, he would “get it straightened out”.

(Reporting by Dan Peleschuk, writing by Yuliia DysaEditing by Ros Russell)

items.title: Starlink in Ukraine back to normal after week of throttling
items.author: Yuliia Dysa
items.creator: Yuliia Dysa
items.summary: A week of restrictions disrupted military operations and intensified tensions with the US.
items.body:
Ukraine said on Saturday that the Starlink satellite system and its military version Starshield were now fully functional after over a week of restrictions that disrupted military operations and intensified tensions with the US.
Problems with Elon Musk's SpaceX-owned systems came after US President Donald Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel while pressing Kyiv to stop striking Russian oil refineries.
Ukrainian officials said the restrictions, which capped operations at speeds of 160 kilometres per hour (kph), hampered the military's ability to intercept Russian attack drones and forced the cancellation of some operations.
"The main thing for today is that Starlink and Starshield have resumed operations at their pre-restriction speeds. The speeds are now at the level we need," President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on the Telegram app.
According to Zelenskiy, the speeds started returning to normal overnight. Ukraine's defence ministry said on Saturday the connection remained stable at over 400 kph.
Ukraine does not rely on the systems for long-range drone operations on Russian territory, including attacks on refineries.
But Starlink remains [USN:L6N4690ON TEXT:"vital"] for frontline communications, and the deployment of Starshield-enabled medium-range attack drones has helped Ukraine gain the upper hand in several areas of the battlefield this year.
LIMITATIONS ORDER The restrictions sparked outrage in Ukraine, particularly as they coincided with disruptions to allied warnings about incoming Russian missile attacks. Kyiv later said it continued to receive US intelligence.
Neither Musk nor the US government has acknowledged responsibility for restricting Starlink or Starshield in Ukraine. Both have said publicly that any such decision could only have been taken by the other.
Reuters has reported that the [USN:L1N4610ZC TEXT:"order to throttle"] Starshield came from inside the White House. Previously, US administrations had several times [USN:L4N4691IH TEXT:"asked SpaceX"] to turn Starlink on or off in various countries, sources said.
On Friday, contradicting his previous statement that the services had been fully restored, Trump said that if problems persisted, he would "[USN:L6N4690ZQ TEXT:"get it straightened out"]".

items.title: Kotak Mahindra Bank's Q2 consolidated net profit rises 26% to ₹5,645 crore
items.author: Subrata Panda
items.summary: Standalone profit rose 29 per cent as NII grew 16 per cent and provisions fell, though large FCNR(B) inflows pushed net interest margin down to 4.31 per cent ...
items.body: Kotak Mahindra Bank on Saturday reported a 26 per cent year-on-year (YoY) rise in consolidated net profit to ₹5,645 crore for the July-September quarter of FY27 (Q2FY27), from ₹4,468 crore in Q2FY26. Sequentially, profit was up 3 per cent from ₹5,480 crore in the June quarter (Q1FY27). On a standalone basis, the bank reported a 29 per cent YoY rise in net profit to ₹4,212 crore for the September quarter (Q2FY27). The rise came on lower provisions and 16 per cent growth in net interest income (NII), even as the bank's margin contracted on inflows of foreign currency non-resident (bank) [FCNR(B)] deposits. The bank had reported a net profit of ₹3,253 crore in Q2FY26. Sequentially, profit was up 2 per cent from ₹4,123 crore in Q1FY27. Net interest income (NII) rose 16 per cent YoY to ₹8,459 crore from ₹7,311 crore in Q2FY26. Sequentially, it was up 7 per cent from ₹7,928 crore in Q1FY27. Net interest margin (NIM) stood at 4.31 per cent, against 4.54 per cent a year earlier and 4.53 per cent in Q1. The bank said the moderation was largely on account of FCNR(B) mobilisation during the quarter.  It raised FCNR(B) deposits of about ₹55,344 crore and extended loans of about ₹16,110 crore through its international branches.  Cost of funds was 4.52 per cent in Q2FY27, compared with 4.70 per cent a year ago and 4.46 per cent in Q1. Fee and services income rose 21 per cent YoY to ₹2,926 crore in Q2FY27.  Operating expenses increased 14 per cent to ₹5,271 crore.  Provisions fell 15 per cent YoY to ₹803 crore from ₹947 crore, though they were higher than ₹668 crore in Q1.  Annualised credit cost was 0.35 per cent, against 0.79 per cent in Q2FY26 and 0.46 per cent in Q1. Asset quality of the bank improved. Slippages declined 24 per cent to ₹1,230 crore in Q2FY27 from ₹1,629 crore in the year-ago period. Gross non-performing assets (GNPA) were 1.04 per cent of advances as of September 30, against 1.39 per cent a year earlier. Net NPA was 0.24 per cent, against 0.32 per cent in Q2FY26. The provision coverage ratio stood at 78 per cent, compared with 77 per cent in the year-ago quarter. Net advances grew 25 per cent to ₹5.77 trillion in Q2FY27. Excluding loans against FCNR(B) deposits and the loan portfolio acquired from Kotak Mahindra Investments (KMIL), growth was 19 per cent.  Total deposits rose 23 per cent to ₹6.51 trillion, or 13 per cent excluding FCNR(B) deposits, in the July-Sept quarter of FY27. The current account and savings account (CASA) ratio fell to 38.2 per cent in Q2FY27 from 42.3 per cent a year ago, which the bank attributed to the increase in term deposits from FCNR(B) inflows. Excluding these deposits, the ratio was 41.8 per cent. The credit-to-deposit ratio was 88.6 per cent in Q2FY27, compared with 87.5 per cent in the year-ago period. Standalone annualised return on assets (ROA) was 1.92 per cent and return on equity (ROE) was 11.65 per cent. The capital adequacy ratio was 21.9 per cent, with a CET1 ratio of 21.4 per cent. For the quarter under review, among subsidiaries, Kotak Securities reported a profit of ₹348 crore and Kotak Mahindra Prime ₹251 crore. Kotak Mahindra Life Insurance posted a profit of ₹198 crore. Kotak Asset Management and Trustee Company earned ₹287 crore in profit, while Kotak Alternate Asset Managers earned ₹87 crore in profit. (Disclosure: Entities controlled by the Kotak family have a significant holding in Business Standard Pvt Ltd)

items.title: Indonesia cuts pipeline gas exports to Singapore by about 9%
items.author: Reuters
items.creator: Reuters
items.summary: Indonesia cut 31 million standard cubic feet of gas per day (mmscfd) from its pipeline natural gas exports to Singapore starting on Saturday to divert supply to the domestic power sector, upstream oil and gas regulator SKK Migas said.
items.body:
Indonesia cut 31 million standard cubic feet of gas per day (mmscfd) from its pipeline natural gas exports to Singapore starting on Saturday to divert supply to the domestic power sector, upstream oil and gas regulator SKK Migas said.
Indonesia cut 15 mmscfd from its supply to Singapore from Natuna and another 16 mmscfd of gas from Sumatra, SKK Migas chairman Djoko Siswanto told Reuters on Saturday.
Singapore's Energy Market Authority said the total reduction amounts to 17 bbtud over a period of 18 days, which is "less than 2% of our total daily gas demand of more than 1,000 bbtud".
"EMA understands that our importers will pursue all relevant recourse in their contracts for the gas supply disruption," the Energy Market Authority spokesperson said
Singapore's Energy Market Authority said state gas buyer GasCo is ready to import more LNG at any time and that the country has sufficient energy supplies for national demand
Most of Indonesia’s gas exports to Singapore are delivered via pipeline, and the cuts would account for around 9% of that supply
“In order to safeguard the reliability of domestic gas supplies for electricity generation, effective today, gas supplies previously destined for Singapore are being redirected for domestic use,” said Djoko
The gas is being redirected to meet electricity needs in Batam, Bintan and Sumatra, he said
Batam and several cities in Indonesia's Riau Islands province suffered a [USN:L4N46103P TEXT:"blackout"] that lasted 16 hours earlier this month
[USN:L6N4680QU TEXT:"Indonesia energy minister"] Bahlil Lahadalia earlier this week said he would prioritise natural resources use for domestic needs, and review contracts to maintain energy security
[USN:L4N45T0LE TEXT:"Singapore generates"] up to 95% of its electricity from natural gas

items.title: Houthis say they attacked Saudi oil sites; strikes reported in Aden
items.author: Reuters
items.creator: Reuters
items.summary: Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis said they launched attacks on Saudi oil facilities and airports on Saturday, and the Saudi-led coalition fighting the group said it downed two missiles, as clashes between the two sides intensified.
items.body:
Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis said they launched attacks on Saudi oil facilities and airports on Saturday, and the Saudi-led coalition fighting the group said it downed two missiles, as clashes between the two sides intensified.
On another front of an escalating conflict reignited by the Iran war , Yemen's Saudi-backed government said the Houthis also fired three ballistic missiles at coast guard sites in the southern Yemeni port city of Aden.
Saudi authorities did not comment directly on the Houthi statements, though they reported missile debris falling near the site of one of the purported oil targets. It was not immediately clear if any of the reported attacks had hit their targets in the kingdom or had been intercepted.
SAUDIS REPORT DEBRIS FROM INTERCEPTED MISSILES Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, an Aramco facility in Yanbu, the Rabigh oil refinery, crude oil pumping stations and the East-West Pipeline.
He also said the group targeted King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, an airport in Najran and an airbase in Khamis Mushait.
The Saudi-led coalition earlier said it destroyed two ballistic missiles fired by Houthis towards Yanbu and Taif.
Saudi Civil Defense said debris from intercepted missiles had fallen in the Mecca and Medina regions, home to Islam's holiest sites visited by millions of Muslim pilgrims every year.
It said parts of the intercepted missiles fell in Wadi al-Mughammas in Mecca, while debris also fell in areas in Jeddah, Taif and Rabigh. It was not clear if that was linked to the Houthis' reported targeting of Rabigh oil refinery.
The renewed fighting has shattered a 2022 UN-brokered truce that largely halted cross-border attacks between the Saudi-led coalition, which backs Yemen's internationally recognised government, and the Houthis, who control the capital Sanaa.
The escalation has opened another front in the US-Israeli war on Iran .
In Yemen, the Interior Ministry of the internationally recognised government said two of the Houthis' missiles had struck a coast guard headquarters, while a third hit a coast guard building in the Tawahi district.
Houthi spokesman Saree said the group's forces had targeted Saudi-backed military gatherings at what he called Al-Nasr camp and a naval military base in Aden, saying Saudi officers were overseeing the mobilisation there.
There was no immediate comment from the Saudi-led coalition on that assertion.
Earlier on Saturday, Saudi Arabia's Civil Defense briefly issued alerts warning residents of potential danger in Taif and Yanbu, as well as in the holy city of Mecca and the kingdom's second-largest city, Jeddah.
About 10 minutes later, the agency said the threat had passed.
The Houthis warned airlines earlier this month against using Saudi airspace, exempting only the airspace over Mecca and Medina, as they intensified attacks on the kingdom.

items.title: 金総書記1年ぶり訪中、今月開通の国境橋使用　習指導部要人と会談
items.author: ロイター
items.creator: ロイター
items.summary: ［ソウル／北京　２４日　ロイター］ -
items.body:
［ソウル／北京　２４日　ロイター］ - 北朝鮮の金正恩朝鮮労働党総書記は２４日、中国遼寧省丹東を訪問した。中国国営新華社が伝えた。金氏の訪中は２０２５年９月以来、約１年ぶり。中国共産党序列４位の王滬寧・人民政治協商会議（政協）主席が金氏を迎え、会談で習近平国家主席のメッセージを伝えた。

金氏は、今月開通したばかりの、中朝を結ぶ新鴨緑江大橋を渡って丹東に到着した。中国国営中央テレビ（ＣＣＴＶ）の映像には、旗を振る人々が並ぶ橋の上を、金氏が北朝鮮側へ歩く様子が映っていた。

今回の訪問は、１９５０─５３年の朝鮮戦争に中国人民義勇軍が参戦した日の前日というタイミングで、新華社によると、金氏は王氏とともに丹東の朝鮮戦争記念施設を訪れた。当地の自動車工場も視察したという。 

一連の予定を終えた金氏は北朝鮮に戻った。韓国聯合ニュースは、王氏が新鴨緑江大橋で見送ったと伝えた。

２５年９月の訪中時は、北京で開かれた戦勝８０周年の記念行事に出席し、習近平国家主席と会談した。習氏は今年６月に北朝鮮を公式訪問した。

トランプ米大統領は北朝鮮との対話再開に意欲を示している。１１月には中国・深センでアジア太平洋経済協力会議（ＡＰＥＣ）首脳会議が開催され、トランプ氏も出席する予定だ。 

＜中朝経済関係強化＞ 

中国は、北朝鮮にとって経済・外交面の主要な後ろ盾で、北朝鮮の公式な貿易の大半を占めている。ただ、ロシアが２０２２年にウクライナに侵攻して以降、北朝鮮はロシアとの軍事関係を深めており、中国への依存が弱まったのではないかとの見方が専門家から出ている。今回の訪中は、中朝が経済関係の強化に改めて取り組んでいることを印象付けた。

新鴨緑江大橋は今月１５日に開通した。橋自体は１４年に完成したが、北朝鮮側の準備が整わず、開通が遅れた。

新しい橋は、北朝鮮が開発に必要とする重機や原材料、エネルギー製品の輸送に役立つと期待されている。王氏は金氏との会談で、中国は橋の開通を機に人的交流や経済・貿易協力を拡大する用意があると伝えた。 

オランダのライデン大学で朝鮮半島を専門とするクリストファー・グリーン氏は、橋の開通の遅れは中朝関係がいかに機能不全に陥っていたかを示すと指摘した上で、「金氏は新鴨緑江大橋を渡って中国に入ることで、２国間貿易にお墨付きを与えた」と述べた。

中国政府系シンクタンク、遼寧社会科学院で中朝関係を研究する呂超氏は、金氏の訪中は、中朝の経済関係が緊密になり、ハイレベル交流が頻繁に行われている現在の流れに沿ったものだと述べた。「橋の開通で、物流の制約が和らぎ、２国間貿易はさらに増える可能性が高い」と語った。

items.title: Jordan king orders 'iron fist' response to deadly church attack
items.author: Abdelhadi Ramahi
items.creator: Abdelhadi Ramahi
items.summary: Jordan's King Abdullah ordered security forces on Saturday to respond with an "iron fist" as authorities searched for gunmen who opened fire and killed nine people during a church funeral service.
items.body:
Jordan's King Abdullah ordered security forces on Saturday to respond with an "iron fist" as authorities searched for gunmen who opened fire and killed nine people during a church funeral service.
The assailants [USN:L6N46A02E TEXT:"fired for several minutes"] in broad daylight at the church in Karak governorate on Friday, and also wounded 40 people in the rare attack on Jordan's Christian minority.
Security was stepped up at malls, foreign embassies and other locations across the country, the US embassy in Amman said.
'A SENSE OF PANIC TOOK HOLD' A priest described how he and others ordered people to get to the ground at Saint George's Greek Orthodox church, about 120 km (75 miles) southwest of the capital, Amman.
"A sense of panic took hold among those present," Theodoros Soueiss told Reuters. "The gunfire was indiscriminate, and you never knew where a bullet might land."
King Abdullah condemned the "despicable terrorist act" as he chaired a National Security Council meeting and said there was no room for leniency when it comes to the lives of Jordanians, the royal court said.
Such attacks are highly unusual in Jordan, a relatively stable state in the Middle East, though authorities there say they have foiled several Islamist plots in recent years.
There was no immediate claim of responsibility for the attack in the kingdom, a major partner with the US in the fight against militant groups.
Officials have said it is too early to determine whether the attackers had links to known groups inside or outside Jordan.
"A massacre, a massacre in every sense of the word," said Tarek Ammarin at a hospital where the wounded were being treated. A relative of Ammarin's was injured in the attack.
Christians make up a minority of Jordan's population. The country is home to several biblical sites that attract Christian pilgrims from around the world.
Jordan has been among the US allies in the Middle East to be hit by Iranian attacks this year after the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran in February.
Bahjat al-Rushda, mayor of Shihan village in Karak, joined a long list of officials condemning what they called an attack by extremist terrorists.
"God willing, this country will remain secure," he said.

items.title: North Korea's Kim crosses new bridge into China as trade ties warm
items.author: Joyce Lee, Eduardo Baptista
items.creator: Joyce Lee, Eduardo Baptista
items.summary: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visited the Chinese border city of Dandong on Saturday, Xinhua reported, crossing a newly opened bridge in a symbolic move seen as highlighting Beijing and Pyongyang's push to expand trade ties.
items.body:
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visited the Chinese border city of Dandong on Saturday, Xinhua reported, crossing a newly opened bridge in a symbolic move seen as highlighting Beijing and Pyongyang's push to expand trade ties.
Kim was accompanied during his visit by China's fourth-highest-ranked official Wang Huning, who conveyed greetings from President Xi Jinping, the official Xinhua news agency said.
Kim arrived in Dandong via the [USN:L6N46004I TEXT:"New Yalu River Bridge"] connecting North Korea and China , a South Korean government official said on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to speak publicly.
The new bridge is expected to help move heavy equipment, raw materials and energy products that North Korea needs for development. Its official opening this month is the latest sign of warming ties between Beijing and Pyongyang, after two summits between their leaders in the past 13 months.
China, which fought alongside North Korea in the 1950-1953 Korean War, remains Pyongyang's main economic and diplomatic backer and accounts for most of its official trade.
CHINESE TV SHOWS KIM WALKING ON BRIDGE But North Korea's deepening military ties with Russia since Moscow's 2022 invasion of Ukraine have led analysts to question whether Pyongyang is becoming less reliant on Beijing.
Kim's trip nevertheless points to a renewed push by China and North Korea to bolster their economic relationship.
South Korea's Yonhap news agency had earlier reported that Kim was expected to return to North Korea after Saturday's visit.
Footage from Chinese state broadcaster CCTV showed Kim walking on the bridge, lined by people waving flags, towards North Korea.
Xinhua said Wang accompanied Kim to a Korean War memorial in Dandong, where the North Korean leader paid tribute to Chinese People's Volunteer Army soldiers who fought alongside North Korea during the three-year conflict. Kim also toured a Dandong [USN:RTV844HDK TEXT:"automobile factory"], it said.
NEW YALU RIVER BRIDGE BOOSTS BILATERAL TIES China and North Korea opened the 3 km (2 mile) New Yalu River Bridge, their most significant [USN:L1N46103M TEXT:"land border crossing"], this month after a long delay, aiming to rejuvenate trade and commerce after years of strained ties and pandemic-related disruptions.
"Kim has given his imprimatur to bilateral trade by crossing the New Yalu River Bridge to enter China," said Christopher Green, a Korea specialist at Leiden University in the Netherlands, saying the delayed opening had shown how dysfunctional the relationship had become.
During a meeting on Saturday, Wang told Kim that China was ready to use the bridge's opening to expand personnel exchanges and economic and trade cooperation, Xinhua said.
A visit by Kim now is consistent with the current phase of closer economic ties and more frequent high-level exchanges between China and North Korea, said Lu Chao, an expert in China-North Korea relations at the Liaoning Academy of Social Sciences, a Chinese government think-tank in Shenyang.
"The opening of the bridge has resolved a major bottleneck in China-North Korea trade logistics," Lu said. "With the logistics constraint eased, bilateral trade is likely to increase further."
TRUMP WAITS FOR KIM TO ENGAGE Kim's last known visit to China was in September 2025, to attend the 80th Victory Day celebrations in Beijing, when he held a summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping. Xi made a [USN:L1N42G106 TEXT:"state visit"] to North Korea in June.
US President Donald Trump has been eager to jump-start talks with North Korea, but US and South Korean officials see [USN:L1N4690EW TEXT:"fading chances"] of him meeting Kim this year, Reuters reported on Friday.
China hosts a summit of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum next month in Shenzhen, which Trump is expected to attend.

items.title: 米英首脳が電話会談、北海油田やウクライナ・フォークランド巡り協議
items.author: ロイター
items.creator: ロイター
items.summary: ［ワシントン　２３日　ロイター］ -
items.body:
［ワシントン　２３日　ロイター］ - トランプ米大統領は２３日、バーナム英首相と電話会談し、北海油田の開発について協議したと明らかにした。イランやウクライナの紛争についても「ごく軽く」触れたとしている。

トランプ氏は、中間選挙に向けフロリダ州での遊説に出発する前、ホワイトハウスで記者団に対し「彼らは北海油田を開放しようとしている」と述べた。「私は２年間それを求めてきた。アンディ（・バーナム氏）がそれを実現しつつある」と語った。

トランプ氏は２１日、英国が北海のジャックドー・ガス田の開発を承認したことを称賛した。

英首相府の声明によると、バーナム氏はまた、フォークランド諸島沖の石油探査問題も取り上げた。同諸島は英国の海外領土で広範な自治権を持つが、アルゼンチンが長年にわたり領有権を主張している。

バーナム氏はウクライナを巡り、ロシアに対して自衛するためにウクライナがスターリンクへの全面的なアクセスを確保することの重要性を強調した。また、ロシアのプーチン大統領を交渉の席に着かせようとするトランプ氏の努力を歓迎した。

両首脳は中東についても協議し、バーナム氏はフーシ派の攻撃に直面するサウジアラビアへの英国の支持を改めて表明したという。

items.title: How Trump's energy dominance turned into hubris
items.author: Ron Bousso
items.creator: Ron Bousso
items.summary: It was the US position as the world's top oil and gas producer that enabled Trump to pursue foreign-policy goals that may turn out to be the costliest of his political career.
items.body:
When Donald Trump returned to the White House in 2025, [USN:L1N3Q1127 TEXT:"“energy dominance”"] was the bedrock of his economic and foreign policy plans. But an unpopular war with Iran and soaring household fuel costs have now made energy policy a major liability for the US president heading into next month’s midterm elections .
Ironically, it was the US position as the world's top oil and gas producer, perhaps more than anything else, that enabled Trump to pursue foreign policy goals that may turn out to be the costliest of his political career.
In the first two years of Trump’s second term, vast US oil and gas resources emboldened Washington abroad, strengthened its hand in trade disputes and underpinned a broader effort to restore US geopolitical dominance.
Yet the Iran war exposed the central weakness in that vision: dominating energy production does not mean controlling energy prices.
What began as a pursuit of US energy independence evolved into a doctrine of energy dominance. That is now looking like energy hubris.
UNLEASHING AMERICAN ENERGY The foundations of Trump’s strategy were laid long before his return to office last year. The development of cost-effective techniques to tap the country's onshore shale basins transformed the US into the world’s largest producer of natural gas in 2009 and petroleum in 2018. By 2022, it was the leading exporter of liquefied natural gas, giving Washington unprecedented influence over global energy markets.
US crude production rose from around 5.5 million barrels per day in 2010 to nearly 14 million bpd today, around a fifth of global supplies, while the country also accounts for more than a quarter of global LNG exports. No single nation has ever occupied such a commanding position in the global energy system.
Trump sought to turn that advantage into a governing doctrine.
On his first day back in office, he declared a national energy emergency and ordered the government to [USN:S0N3NI004 TEXT:"“unleash American energy”"], prioritising oil, gas, coal and nuclear power while sidelining renewables.
Within weeks, he made “energy dominance” official US policy, establishing the National Energy Dominance Council and reviving his familiar “drill, baby, drill” slogan as the purported cure for elevated inflation and economic anxiety. In an October 2025 proclamation, Trump summed up the philosophy as “maximum production, maximum prosperity, and maximum power”.
ENERGY POLICY IS FOREIGN POLICY This doctrine extended far beyond domestic energy policy.
The administration’s national security strategy, published last December, explicitly linked US influence in the Western Hemisphere to energy dominance, drawing on the 19th-century Monroe Doctrine that sought to oppose European political intervention in the region.
In a little over a year, the administration wielded US oil and LNG exports in trade negotiations, promoted energy deals as part of efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war , and highlighted Greenland’s resource wealth in a push for greater influence over the [USN:L6N45E05Y TEXT:"Arctic territory"].
The high-water mark for Trump’s energy doctrine arguably came early this year after [USN:L6N3Y407K TEXT:"Washington removed Venezuelan President"] Nicolas Maduro in a swift military operation.
The US subsequently [USN:L1N3ZM1KL TEXT:"took control"] of Venezuelan oil exports and revenues, forced through changes to the country’s hydrocarbons legislation that displaced Chinese companies, and secured an unprecedented agreement granting it access to a fifth of Venezuela’s oil reserves.
By February, Trump’s vision of building an economy and foreign policy around abundant fossil fuel resources appeared to be taking root. The US possessed not only more energy than any rival, but also the ability to use that abundance to shape trade, diplomacy and security.
Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran in late February put that doctrine to the test.
THE IRAN QUAGMIRE The president initially claimed that the joint campaign with Israel against Iran would last only a few weeks. He also repeatedly indicated that vast US oil and gas resources, together with newfound access to Venezuela’s oil wealth, would shield the economy from any resulting spike in energy costs, which he also suggested would be brief.
Those assumptions have not aged well.
The war launched on February 28 led to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly one-fifth of global energy supplies used to flow, triggering one of the largest energy disruptions in modern history. Middle Eastern producers cut output and rerouted exports where possible, while major importers across Asia reduced consumption.
This caused oil prices to nearly double in the first two months of the conflict, with global benchmark Brent crude peaking at $118 a barrel in March.
That was well below the record [USN:L03220220 TEXT:"$145 reached in 2008"], when Iran-related geopolitical tensions, surging Chinese demand and a weakening US dollar drove prices higher. It was also far less than many had feared, largely thanks to reduced Chinese oil imports, ample crude stocks and the surprising adaptability of global markets. But it still represented a severe shock.
Moreover, the risk premium from the Iran war is becoming entrenched. Even though crude flows from the Middle East have mostly recovered, Brent is trading around $110.
The conflict has also spread across the Middle East, pulling in most of Washington's Gulf allies, most notably the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia, which have suffered multiple deadly attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis. This has upended the market’s confidence in the security of Middle Eastern crude, unravelled longstanding supply routes and sent [USN:L6N45R160 TEXT:"shipping prices"] skyrocketing.
Trump wanted to put his stamp on global energy markets, but this was clearly not what he had in mind.
PAIN AT THE PUMP In one respect, the 2026 energy shock has vindicated Trump’s strategy. The war cemented the US position as the world’s top supplier of crude, refined fuels and LNG, delivering enormous profits to domestic producers and exporters and allowing the US to expand its position in the global market.
Energy independence certainly offered US consumers some protection against the energy shock, particularly compared with Asian economies, where prices and demand destruction were much more extreme this year.
But that protection has been far from ironclad.
US gasoline prices at the pump climbed above $4.60 a gallon in May, the highest level since 2022, while [USN:L1N45211Q TEXT:"diesel"] surged to a record $6.50 a gallon in September as global refining capacity was squeezed.
Those increases rapidly became a political problem for the White House as cost-of-living concerns moved to the forefront of the campaign ahead of the midterms on November 3.
The administration sought to contain the fuel-price spike by pulling almost every available lever, including [USN:L6N44M0V8 TEXT:"easing biofuel blending mandates"] and, most controversially, reaching a [USN:L4N45Y0AR TEXT:"diesel supply agreement"] with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
This dynamic underscores the difference between commanding supply and controlling prices.
Oil, LNG and refined fuels are internationally traded commodities. US producers sell them at prices shaped by global supply and demand. They don’t typically reserve cheap energy for American households.
While Trump briefly floated the idea of a [USN:L6N45E0T3 TEXT:"diesel export ban"], officials ultimately rejected it. Even though a ban might have brought down domestic prices initially, it would likely have resulted in higher fuel prices over the medium term due to global market dynamics.
‘ENERGY SECURITY IS NATIONAL SECURITY’ The administration’s assertion last October that “energy security is national security” appears more relevant than ever. The Iran war has shown that cheap and reliable energy is essential for economic growth, whether it powers heavy industry or the data centres underpinning the artificial intelligence race.
But the conflict has also changed the meaning of energy security.
For countries dependent on imports, particularly [USN:L6N3ZY18D TEXT:"many in Asia"], the shock has revealed the risks of relying heavily on distant suppliers, vulnerable shipping routes and a concentrated global refining system. Their response is likely to be broader diversification: securing more suppliers, expanding domestic fossil fuel production where possible, accelerating renewable power and shifting more transport towards electricity.
That will not kick the US off its lofty energy perch, but it will likely weaken the allure of oil and gas for many countries over the coming years.
Trump likely felt emboldened to embark on the Iran war — something his predecessors had baulked at — precisely because US energy independence made a Middle East adventure seem less risky than it had when the US was heavily reliant on Gulf oil and gas.
But the conflict has, perhaps permanently, undermined Trump’s promise that energy dominance would guarantee low prices and economic security at home.
Hubris can be a dangerous thing.
(The opinions expressed here are those of Ron Bousso , a columnist for Reuters.)

items.title: ＧＭＯ、政府に能動的サイバー防御要請　金銭の要求には応じず
items.author: ロイター
items.creator: ロイター
items.summary:
Kentaro Okasaka

[東京 ２４日 ロイター] -
items.body:
Kentaro Okasaka

[東京 ２４日 ロイター] - ＧＭＯインターネットは２４日、自社のＦＸ（外国為替証拠金取引）の自動売買サービスが受けたサイバー攻撃について、「能動的サイバー防御」の適用を政府に緊急要請したと発表した。攻撃者とみられる相手から同社に対し金銭の要求があり、応じなければ自社や顧客の情報を公開するとの連絡を受けたという。

要求には応じない方針。警察などと連携して対応するとしている。また、サービスの全利用者に一律５０００円の見舞金を支払うことを決めた。

能動的サイバー防御は、被害が深刻化する前に国や関係機関が主導して攻撃者のインフラや侵入経路を特定し、無力化して被害の未然防止を図る仕組み。同社は今回の事案について、一般国民の取引口座（金融資産）を標的とした不正操作・資産毀損という「極めて悪質かつ前例のない手口」だと判断。政府に先制的な対応を求めることを決めた。

同社によると、今月１９日に顧客からの問い合わせを受け調査を開始。２０日にサービスの一部顧客のサーバー環境への不正なプログラムの設置を確認し、２１日には被害拡大防止のため全プランのサーバーを順次停止した。顧客から取引口座での身に覚えのない操作などの報告があり、２２日に警察へ相談したという。

Kentaro Okasaka

[東京 ２４日 ロイター] - ＧＭＯインターネットは２４日、自社のＦＸ（外国為替証拠金取引）の自動売買サービスが受けたサイバー攻撃について、「能動的サイバー防御」の適用を政府に緊急要請したと発表した。攻撃者とみられる相手から同社に対し金銭の要求があり、応じなければ自社や顧客の情報を公開するとの連絡を受けたという。

要求には応じない方針。警察などと連携して対応するとしている。また、サービスの全利用者に一律５０００円の見舞金を支払うことを決めた。

能動的サイバー防御は、被害が深刻化する前に国や関係機関が主導して攻撃者のインフラや侵入経路を特定し、無力化して被害の未然防止を図る仕組み。同社は今回の事案について、一般国民の取引口座（金融資産）を標的とした不正操作・資産毀損という「極めて悪質かつ前例のない手口」だと判断。政府に先制的な対応を求めることを決めた。

同社によると、今月１９日に顧客からの問い合わせを受け調査を開始。２０日にサービスの一部顧客のサーバー環境への不正なプログラムの設置を確認し、２１日には被害拡大防止のため全プランのサーバーを順次停止した。顧客から取引口座での身に覚えのない操作などの報告があり、２２日に警察へ相談したという。

items.title: 米司法省、アラスカ上院選の結果認定阻止へ訴訟　「候補者名酷似」理由に
items.author: ロイター
items.creator: ロイター
items.summary: ［２３日　ロイター］ -
items.body:
［２３日　ロイター］ - 米司法省は２２日、１１月中間選挙のアラスカ州連邦上院選で共和党の現職候補が僅差で敗北した場合に、州による選挙結果の認定を差し止めるよう求める訴訟を起こした。投票用紙にほぼ同姓同名の共和党候補が２人記載されており、有権者の混乱を招く恐れがあると主張している。

アラスカは共和党が上院多数派を維持できるかを左右する可能性のある州の一つで、共和党の現職ダン・Ｓ・サリバン氏が、民主党のメアリー・ペルトラ氏と接戦を繰り広げている。

司法省は、選挙にダン・Ｊ・サリバン・ジュニアという名の共和党候補が出馬していることを問題視。訴状は、同氏が「サリバン上院議員の支持者を誤って自身に投票させる意図を持って」立候補していると主張している。

司法省は訴状で、「有権者の混乱の影響を受けた可能性がある」結果の認定を差し止めるよう要請。これにより「ダニエル・Ｊ・サリバン氏に投じられた票が本来はサリバン上院議員に投じられるはずだったものかどうかを調べる調査」が可能になるとしている。

トランプ大統領は２３日、記者団に対して、訴訟を支持すると述べ「やれと言ったのは私だ」と語った。

items.title: ＭＬＢ＝ＷＳ開幕、ブルワーズが先勝　ミジオロウスキーが最速記録
items.author: ロイター
items.creator: ロイター
items.summary: ［２３日　ロイター］ -
items.body:
［２３日　ロイター］ - 米大リーグ（ＭＬＢ）は２３日、ワールドシリーズ（ＷＳ、７回戦制）の第１戦を行い、ブルワーズがレイズを３─２で下し、先勝した。

１９８２年以来４４年ぶりのＷＳ出場となったブルワーズは一回、指名打者クリスチャン・イエリチの適時三塁打で先制し、ウィリアム・コントレラス捕手の適時打で２点目を挙げた。

四回に１点を返されたが、七回にはジャクソン・チョウリオ外野手の適時打で１点を追加。九回には１点差に迫られ、２死二、三塁のピンチを迎えたものの、４番手トレバー・メギル投手が最後の打者を三振に仕留めた。

先発ジェーコブ・ミジオロウスキー投手は５回を投げ、４安打１失点、１四球、３三振で勝利投手となった。試合の初球に時速１０３．５マイル（約１６６．６キロ）を計測し、球速の計測が始まった２００８年以降のＷＳ最速記録を樹立した。

items.title: 北朝鮮の金総書記、「軍事革命」加速を要求　精鋭部隊育成へ
items.author: ロイター
items.creator: ロイター
items.summary: ［ソウル　２４日　ロイター］ -
items.body:
［ソウル　２４日　ロイター］ - 北朝鮮の金正恩朝鮮労働党総書記は、平壌で２日間にわたり開かれた朝鮮人民軍の中隊長会議で、各中隊を自立して戦闘を遂行できる精鋭部隊にするよう求めた。朝鮮中央通信（ＫＣＮＡ）が２４日に伝えた。

今回の会議は、軍事力強化を一貫して政策の優先課題とする金氏の姿勢を鮮明にした。

金氏は１０月２２─２３日に開かれた会議で演説し、「新時代の軍備増強の目標」の達成に向け、全ての中隊が万全の準備を整えるよう求めた。ＫＣＮＡによると、２月の第９回朝鮮労働党大会以降、全軍規模の会議が開かれたのは初めて。

金氏は「最強の軍隊を建設し、われわれの方式による軍事革命を加速させよう」と述べた。

今後５年間の国家の方向性を定める２月の第９回党大会で、金氏は通常戦力の強化を求めるとともに、核兵器とミサイルの開発を進める方針を改めて示していた。

items.title: ＮＢＡ＝八村、古巣レーカーズ戦で16得点　クリッパーズは初黒星
items.author: ロイター
items.creator: ロイター
items.summary: ［２３日　ロイター］ -
items.body:
［２３日　ロイター］ - 米プロバスケットボール協会（ＮＢＡ）は２３日、各地で試合を行い、八村塁が先発したクリッパーズはレーカーズに１１７─１２５で敗れ、今季初黒星を喫した。

古巣対戦となった八村は計３３分１６秒の出場で、３本の３点シュートを沈めるなど１６得点、６リバウンド、１アシスト、２スチールだった。ダリアス・ガーランドがチーム最多の２６得点を記録した。レーカーズはオースティン・リーブスが２８得点、９アシストで牽引。ルカ・ドンチッチは２３得点、６リバウンド、７アシストも、１１回のターンオーバーを喫した。

セルティックスは昨季王者のニックスに１０７─１０３で競り勝ち、今季初勝利を挙げた。ジェイソン・テイタムが両チーム最多の３６得点に、９リバウンド、７アシストと活躍。ニックスはカールアンソニー・タウンズ、ＯＧ・アヌノビー、マイルズ・マクブライドの３選手が２０得点以上を記録したが及ばなかった。

ロケッツは昨季西地区覇者のスパーズを１１４─１１０で下した。アルペレン・シェングンが両チーム最多の２９得点に、ケビン・デュラントとアメン・トンプソンも２０得点を記録した。スパーズはビクター・ウェンバンヤマが２５得点、１３リバウンドと奮闘した。

ピストンズはヒートに１２８─１１１で勝利し、２連勝とした。ポール・リードが１９得点、１１リバウンド、３アシストのダブルダブルで貢献。ヒートはヤニス・アデトクンボが３６得点、１２リバウンド、５アシストと躍動したが、チーム全体の３点シュート成功率が２９．４％にとどまり、２連敗となった。

ティンバーウルブズはマジックを１１５─９３で下し、２連勝。そのほか、ホークス、ラプターズ、グリズリーズ、トレイルブレイザーズも２連勝とした。

items.title: Trump foreign policy hits voters in the pocketbook, imperiling Republicans in midterms
items.author: Matt Spetalnick
items.creator: Matt Spetalnick
items.summary: Voters are drawing that connection directly, creating a major liability for Donald Trump and imperiling Republicans' control of Congress.
items.body:
Foreign policy is rarely the deciding factor in US midterm elections, when economic considerations usually drive voters’ choices.
But this time, with Donald Trump’s war against Iran and his sweeping tariff campaign pushing up costs for Americans, a president’s approach to world affairs has itself become a pocketbook issue.
As the November 3 elections approach, there are growing signs that voters are drawing that connection directly, creating a major liability for Trump and his fellow Republicans and imperiling their control of Congress.
Those include a Reuters/Ipsos poll earlier this month showing some 78% of Americans [USN:L6N45T0W3 TEXT:"blame Trump's policies"] for rising prices that are outpacing their earnings.
Not since 2006, when President George W. Bush’s Republicans lost both legislative chambers while he was mired in the unpopular Iraq war, has a US leader’s handling of international events appeared so central to shaping the midterms outcome.
The political backlash for Trump could be even bigger, with opinion polls showing that voters feel the economic pain from high gas prices and rising grocery bills in a way that they didn’t two decades ago.
“The bottom line is people are experiencing the impact of Trump’s war and other policies,” said Christopher Preble, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center think tank in Washington. “Now voters have a chance to register their discontent with how he’s dealing with all this.”
POLITICS DRIVING FOREIGN POLICY With Trump’s [USN:L6N465159 TEXT:"approval ratings"] touching historic lows, he has left little doubt, despite his public claims to the contrary, that he sees the straight line voters are drawing between his foreign policy and their cost of living.
That has prompted some controversial policy moves in the run-up to the elections.
Chief among them was Trump’s lifting of sanctions on [USN:L4N45Y0AR TEXT:"Russian diesel"] exports aimed at bringing down fuel prices, a step his critics, including some fellow Republicans, say reinforces the impression that he is increasingly siding with Moscow in its war in Ukraine.
He has also pressed Kyiv to halt strikes on [USN:L1N46203J TEXT:"Russian refineries"] as he tries to shift the blame for high US gasoline prices despite experts saying the surge in energy costs is mainly the result of the war he launched alongside Israel against Iran nearly eight months ago.
At the same time, he has promised not to order any [USN:FWN45U1SW TEXT:"new attack"] on Iran before the midterms, though the US and Israel are widely reported to be preparing for a possible major escalation after the elections.
Polls have shown that most voters oppose the war initiated by Trump, who had campaigned on avoiding new foreign interventions. He has insisted Americans should accept temporarily higher gas prices so that he can block Iran from developing a nuclear weapon.
Iran says its nuclear program is for civilian purposes. The UN nuclear watchdog and US intelligence community have assessed that Tehran shuttered a nuclear weapons development program in 2003.
Some Republican candidates have [USN:L4N45N1R0 TEXT:"distanced themselves"] from Trump on matters ranging from the conflict in the Middle East to the trade war with Canada and his pressure campaign against Ukraine.
For its part, Iran has sought to keep oil prices high and hurt Trump in the midterms by deploying new tactics to target ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz and deliberately prolonging the [USN:L8N46515R TEXT:"diplomatic stalemate"], senior Iranian officials have told Reuters.
Defending the administration's approach, White House spokesman Matt Middleton said: "President Trump has always been clear about temporary market disruptions as a result of the conflict in Iran, but the contrast between President Trump’s economic record and Democrats’ ruinous alternative is clear."
‘IT’S THE ECONOMY, STUPID’ Midterm elections historically have been seen as a referendum on the performance of the incumbent in the White House.
And in one election after another in recent decades, the conventional wisdom has been that economic concerns - “it’s the economy, stupid,” as the Clinton-era adage goes - dominate voters’ choices.
Opinion polls for this year’s midterms, including the Reuters/Ipsos survey, show that while voters rank foreign policy low on their list of priorities, it is clear that most Americans see some of Trump’s signature moves on the world stage, such as the Iran war and tariffs, feeding into their higher costs.
Other polls have shown that a majority of Americans have also soured more broadly on Trump’s international approach.
The Chicago Council on Global Affairs said its latest nationwide survey “finds that most Americans believe the Trump administration’s foreign policy actions have negatively impacted America’s global standing and hurt national and household economic conditions.”
Since returning to the White House last year, Trump has shaken up the rules-based global order that Washington helped create from the ashes of World War Two while his relations with allies have steadily worsened and the [USN:L1N45G0ZJ TEXT:"limits of US power"] have been increasingly exposed, analysts say.
LEGISLATIVE BALANCE OF POWER IN PLAY Against this backdrop, Democrats are widely projected to [USN:L6N465159 TEXT:"gain control"] of the House of Representatives in the midterms, with the Senate also seen as increasingly in play.
For Republicans, losing either chamber could complicate Trump's agenda in the last two years of his second term.
But even with a shift in the balance of power on Capitol Hill on November 3, lawmakers will have a hard time reining in Trump’s capacity to pursue foreign policy as he sees fit.
Once the ballots are counted, a big question will be whether Trump will feel either restricted or emboldened on the world stage as he enters what is traditionally considered a lame-duck phase - when a president is barred from running again and no longer faces electoral consequences for decisions made.
“For many presidents who feel politically constrained (at home), foreign policy is the area where they are able to act with relative freedom,” said Jon Alterman of the Center for Strategic and International Studies think tank in Washington.
Analysts say Trump's handling of adversaries such as Iran, Russia, China and even Cuba or his approach to allies across the globe could go either way -- or he could simply lose interest and double down on his string of construction projects, such as the White House ballroom.

items.body: Kotak Mahindra Bank, IDFC First Bank, AU Small Finance Bank, Castrol India, JK Cement, Kajaria Ceramics, Netweb Technologies India, Apollo Micro Systems, Lumax Auto Technologies, Gujarat Ambuja Exports, and SBFC Finance are among the 33 companies scheduled to announce their financial results for the second quarter of the financial year 2026-27 (Q2FY27) on Saturday.  Some other firms announcing their July to September earnings include Chembond Chemicals, Chemcon Speciality Chemicals, High Energy Batteries India, JTL Defence, Rajoo Engineers, Permanent Magnets, Seshasayee Paper and Boards, North Eastern Carrying Corporation, 3P Land Holdings, Modis Navnirman, S V Global Mill, and Damodar Industries. Infosys Q2 result highlightInfosys reported a 6.2 per cent year-on-year rise in net profit to ₹7,828 crore in Q2FY27, while revenue from operations increased 10.7 per cent to ₹49,244 crore. However, the IT services major cut its FY27 revenue growth guidance to 1–2 per cent in constant currency terms from 1.5–3 per cent earlier, citing weaker growth expectations in the US and rising AI-led pricing pressures.  The company reported large deal wins worth $5.2 billion during the quarter, including a mega deal valued at more than $2 billion. AI revenue accounted for 10.5 per cent of total revenue, up from 8.2 per cent in Q1FY27, and grew 29 per cent sequentially. Operating margin remained broadly stable at around 21 per cent, while Infosys retained its FY27 operating margin guidance of 20–22 per cent.Market updates from Oct 23The Sensex and Nifty50 ended lower for the fourth consecutive session as geopolitical tensions weighed on investor sentiment.The Sensex fell 125.56 points, or 0.17 per cent, to 73,123.83, while the Nifty50 declined 87.65 points, or 0.39 per cent, to 22,600. Shriram Finance, Adani Enterprises and JSW Steel were the top losers on the Nifty50. In the broader markets, the Nifty Midcap 100 and Nifty Smallcap 100 fell 2.21 per cent and 2.94 per cent, respectively. Among sectoral indices, Nifty Metal, Nifty Realty and Nifty PSU Bank underperformed, while Nifty IT was the most resilient, declining the least.Companies announcing Q2 results today3P Land Holdings LtdApollo Micro Systems LtdAU Small Finance Bank LtdCastrol India LtdChembond Chemicals LtdChemcon Speciality Chemicals LtdDachepalli Publishers LtdDamodar Industries Ltd-$Evexia Lifecare LtdGujarat Ambuja Exports LtdGerman Green Steel and Power LtdHigh Energy Batteries India LtdIDFC First Bank LtdJK Cement LtdJTL Defence LtdKajaria Ceramics LtdKotak Mahindra Bank LtdLumax Auto Technologies LtdModis Navnirman LtdNorth Eastern Carrying Corporation LtdNetweb Technologies India LtdOswal Yarns LtdPermanent Magnets Ltd-$Quanto Agroworld LtdRajoo Engineers Ltd-$SBFC Finance LtdSaptak Chem And Business LtdSeshasayee Paper and Boards LtdShangar Decor LtdSJ Corporation LtdSKP Securities LtdSovereign Diamonds LtdS V Global Mill Ltd

items.title: Uncovering 'heat storms'
items.summary: Why we needed new language to describe modern heat waves
items.body:
Follow on Apple or Spotify . Listen on the Reuters app.

Reuters reporters set out to define a heat wave and uncovered something far bigger: "heat storms" that now blanket vast stretches of the planet. On this episode of On Assignment, the journalists behind the investigation, Maurice Tamman and Ben Welsh, explain how extreme heat became a constant feature of modern life, and why they needed a new language to describe it.

items.author: ロイター
items.creator: ロイター
items.summary: ［２３日　ロイター］　 -
items.body:
［２３日　ロイター］　 - ソフトバンクグループが出資するデジタル決済企業オーペイは２３日、米国での新規株式公開（ＩＰＯ）で最大４４億２０００万ドルの評価額を目指すと発表した。新興国で拡大するデジタル金融サービスの需要を取り込む狙い。

ナイジェリアを主力市場とするオーペイは、米国預託株式（ＡＤＳ）約１６００万株を１株当たり１９─２１ドルで売り出し、最大３億６６００万ドルの調達を目指す。

米ＩＰＯ市場は、インフレ率の上昇と人工知能（ＡＩ）関連株の急落で圧力にさらされている。新規上場に対する投資家の意欲が後退し、複数の企業が上場計画の延期を余儀なくされる中でのＩＰＯとなる。

オーペイは２０１８年設立。決済、送金、貯蓄、融資などのデジタル金融サービスを提供し、インドネシア、エジプト、パキスタンでも事業を展開している。

世界で６番目に人口が多いナイジェリアは、アフリカ有数のフィンテック市場に成長。調査会社トラクションによると、モニーポイント、フラッターウェーブ、インタースイッチなどのフィンテック企業を輩出している。

提出書類によると、ソフトバンク系企業は今回の売り出し前の時点でオーペイ株の６．６％を保有している。
